title: Plan a farm and select a site

lessons.title: Assessing natural resources
lessons.html:
Start with what the land can do

Farm planning matches enterprises to the land's natural potential, the market and the owner's resources. Choosing the wrong site for an orchard, piggery or dairy can lock a business into losses for decades. A good plan starts with an inventory of natural resources.

Climate

  • Rainfall amount, season (summer or winter rainfall) and reliability.
  • Temperature extremes, frost dates, heat units for crops such as cotton or citrus.
  • Hail, wind and drought risk. Use long-term records from the South African Weather Service or the Agricultural Research Council.

Soils

  • Depth, texture, structure, drainage and water-holding capacity.
  • Chemical status (pH, nutrients, salinity) from laboratory soil analysis.
  • Erodibility and slope. Dig soil profile pits across the farm to map soil forms.

Water

Irrigation and livestock depend on reliable water. Check borehole yields and quality, dam capacity, river flow and existing water use rights. Under the National Water Act 36 of 1998 water use for irrigation and many other purposes must be lawful, either as an existing lawful use, a general authorisation or a licence. Do not plan an irrigation enterprise on water you have no right to use.

Vegetation and topography

Map veld types, carrying capacity, wetlands, riparian zones, invasive alien plants and steep land. Wetlands and steep slopes are generally best protected rather than developed, both for conservation and under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983.

Bring all information together on a farm map (aerial photographs or GIS) showing boundaries, fields, camps, water, soils, roads and infrastructure. This map is the foundation of every later decision.

lessons.title: Selecting sites for enterprises and infrastructure
lessons.html:
Matching sites to purposes

Each enterprise and building has its own site requirements. Use a checklist and score alternatives.

UseSite requirements
Orchards and vineyardsDeep well-drained soil, frost-free slopes (cold air drains to low ground), irrigation water, wind protection
Annual croplandArable soils, gentle slopes, access for machinery
Dairy or feedlotReliable water, good drainage, distance from rivers and neighbours for effluent and odour, all-weather road for milk or feed trucks, electricity
Piggery or poultry housesBiosecurity distance from other units, prevailing wind away from homes, water, power, waste management
Packhouse or storeCentral, on high ground, good road access
HousingSafe from floods, upwind of animal units, access to water and services

Practical factors

  • Access: distance to markets, input suppliers, roads that stay passable in the rainy season.
  • Services: Eskom or alternative electricity, telecoms, labour availability.
  • Legal: zoning, environmental authorisation for certain developments (for example some intensive livestock units or clearing of indigenous vegetation may need approval), water use rights, servitudes.
  • Security against theft of stock and equipment.
  • Flood lines: never build in the floodplain.

Weighted scoring

When choosing between sites, list criteria, give each a weight (e.g. water 30%, soil 25%, access 20%, cost 15%, risk 10%), score each site out of 10 and multiply. The highest total is the best compromise, though any site that fails a critical criterion such as water must be rejected outright.

lessons.title: Drawing up the farm plan
lessons.html:
From inventory to plan

Steps

  1. Set goals: income, lifestyle, risk appetite, succession.
  2. Resource inventory: land, water, capital, labour, skills, machinery.
  3. Market research: which products can be sold profitably and where.
  4. Choose enterprises suited to the land and market, using gross margin budgets to compare them.
  5. Allocate land: divide into land use units (irrigated land, dryland, grazing camps, conservation areas).
  6. Plan infrastructure: fences, water reticulation, roads, buildings, handling facilities.
  7. Financial plan: capital budget, cash flow, financing.
  8. Implementation schedule with priorities and phases.

Camp and water layout

For livestock, design camps so that each has water, with troughs placed to avoid long walks and overgrazing near water. Number of camps should support the planned grazing system with rest periods. Place handling facilities centrally with lanes to camps.

Phasing and risk

Few farms can develop everything at once. Start with the enterprise that brings cash flow soonest and has the lowest risk, then expand. Build in drought reserves and avoid borrowing beyond what cash flow can repay in a poor year.

Example

A 600 ha farm in the Free State with 80 ha of irrigable soil near a river might use the irrigated land for lucerne and maize, the dryland for cash crops in good years and planted pastures, and the veld for a beef herd, with wetlands fenced off. Crop residues feed cattle in winter, linking enterprises.

Key points

  • Base the plan on a full inventory of climate, soils, water and vegetation.
  • Ensure lawful water use under the National Water Act before planning irrigation.
  • Match each enterprise and building to suitable sites using a checklist or weighted scores.
  • Keep buildings out of floodplains and animal units downwind of homes.
  • Phase development and plan for drought.
